items.prompt: Why do your muscles get weaker the longer they keep working, even without any injury?

options.label: Local fuel stores run low and waste products from the effort build up, both making it harder to contract as strongly
options.feedback: That combination of dwindling fuel and rising waste is exactly what makes sustained contraction harder over time.

options.label: The muscle fibres physically shrink the longer they work
options.feedback: A muscle does not shrink over the course of one bout of effort; whatever weakens it happens at a chemical level inside the fibres.

options.label: The bones the muscle pulls on start to bend under repeated strain
options.feedback: Bones are far stiffer than that and do not bend under the load of ordinary sustained effort; the weakening is happening in the muscle, not the bone.

options.label: Nerve signals to the muscle simply stop arriving after a while
options.feedback: Signals keep arriving throughout sustained effort; what changes is how well the muscle itself can respond to them, not whether the signal shows up.

items.ok_line: Dwindling fuel and rising byproducts are exactly what wears the muscle down.
items.ko_title: Not bone, shrinkage, or lost signals
items.ko_line: The weakening happens chemically inside the fibres, not in the bones or the nerve signal itself.
items.exp_text: A working muscle draws on fuel stored close by, and the longer it keeps contracting, the more that local supply is used up and has to be replenished from further away, which cannot keep pace forever. At the same time, the chemical byproducts of all that contracting build up inside the fibres faster than they can be cleared away, interfering with the very process that lets the muscle contract. Between a dwindling fuel supply and a rising build-up of byproducts, the same effort that once felt easy starts to feel like a struggle.

items.prompt: What is happening inside a muscle during a sudden cramp?

options.label: A tendon has snapped, pulling the muscle into a fixed position
options.feedback: A snapped tendon is a distinct and far more serious injury; a cramp resolves on its own within a short time, which a torn tendon never does.

options.label: The muscle locks into an involuntary, sustained contraction, driven by nerve signals firing repeatedly instead of the usual brief, controlled bursts
options.feedback: That repeated misfiring, without a normal release in between, is exactly what locks the muscle into a cramp.

options.label: The muscle has run completely out of blood supply
options.feedback: Blood flow to a cramping muscle is reduced somewhat by the tight contraction itself, but a full loss of blood supply isn't what starts a cramp.

options.label: The bone underneath briefly locks the joint in place
options.feedback: Bones and joints don't lock on their own; what has locked up here is the muscle itself, contracting when it should be relaxing.

items.ok_line: Repeated firing without a release is what locks the muscle up.
items.ko_title: Not a torn tendon or a locked joint
items.ko_line: Nothing has snapped or locked mechanically; the muscle itself is misfiring.
items.exp_title: A signal stuck in the 'on' position
items.exp_text: A muscle normally contracts in brief, controlled bursts, each one followed by a proper release before the next begins. In a cramp, especially in a muscle that is already tired, the nerve signal driving that contraction misfires into a rapid, repeating pattern that doesn't let the muscle relax between bursts, so it locks into one long, involuntary squeeze. Stretching or massaging the muscle can interrupt that misfiring pattern and let the contraction finally let go.

items.prompt: Why can an unfamiliar bout of hard physical effort leave your muscles sore a day or two later, rather than immediately?

options.label: A build-up of waste products stays trapped in the muscle for days
options.feedback: Those byproducts are cleared from the muscle within a short time after effort ends, well before the soreness that follows a couple of days later even begins.

options.label: The muscle is bruised by impact with the bone underneath it
options.feedback: Muscles and the bones beneath them do not collide with each other during exertion; the soreness comes from something happening inside the muscle fibres themselves.

options.label: Tiny tears form in the muscle fibres, and it's the inflammation and repair process afterward, not the tearing itself, that produces the soreness
options.feedback: That repair process, moving in over the following day or so, is exactly what produces the soreness.

options.label: The soreness is simply ordinary tiredness finally catching up
options.feedback: Ordinary tiredness fades within hours; the soreness that shows up a day or two later is a distinct, separate process involving repair inside the muscle.

items.ok_title: Damage that takes a day to hurt
items.ok_line: The repair process, not the original strain, is what produces the ache.
items.ko_line: None of those explains a soreness that only appears a day or two later.
items.exp_title: Damage that takes a day to hurt
items.exp_text: Muscle fibres put under unfamiliar or unusually hard strain can develop tiny tears at a microscopic level, too small to hurt at the moment they happen. Over the following day or so, the body's repair process moves in around that damage, bringing inflammation that swells and sensitises the tissue as it rebuilds the fibres stronger than before. It is that repair process itself, not the original strain, that produces the soreness felt once it is well underway.

items.prompt: During long, hard physical effort, why does the body sometimes divert blood away from the working muscles toward the skin?

options.label: The muscles simply need less blood the longer they work
options.feedback: Working muscles keep needing plenty of blood throughout sustained effort; their demand doesn't drop off, which is exactly what makes this diversion a real trade-off.

options.label: The skin needs extra blood to repair small scrapes picked up during exertion
options.feedback: This diversion happens with or without any scrapes at all; it is about managing heat, not repairing surface injuries.

options.label: Blood moves to the skin to keep it from drying out
options.feedback: Keeping skin from drying out isn't what is driving this shift; the reason is getting rid of heat that is building up inside the body.

options.label: Blood is diverted to the skin to help release the heat building up from sustained effort, competing with the muscles for the same blood supply
options.feedback: That competition for blood, between cooling the skin and supplying the muscles, is exactly what makes this a trade-off.

items.ok_title: A tug of war for blood
items.ok_line: Cooling the skin and fuelling the muscle compete for the same supply.
items.ko_title: Not lower demand or dry skin
items.ko_line: The muscles' demand for blood doesn't fall, and this isn't about moisture or scrapes.
items.exp_title: A tug of war for the same blood supply
items.exp_text: Sustained hard effort generates heat inside the body faster than it can be lost just by sitting still, and one of the body's main ways of shedding that heat is to send more blood flowing near the surface of the skin, where it can cool. That same blood, though, is also needed by the working muscles to keep delivering fuel and oxygen at the rate they are burning through it. Over a long stretch of hard effort, meeting both demands at once becomes a genuine trade-off between staying cool and keeping the muscles fully supplied.

items.prompt: Why can some muscle fibres keep working steadily for a long time while others tire out within seconds?

options.label: Every fibre in a muscle is identical; only blood flow to the whole muscle changes
options.feedback: The fibres within a single muscle are not all alike; different fibres are built with genuinely different properties, not just different blood supply.

options.label: Muscles contain two broad types of fibre: ones built to contract gently but resist fatigue, and ones built for powerful bursts that tire quickly
options.feedback: That split between fatigue-resistant fibres and quick, powerful ones is exactly why different tasks tire the muscle at different rates.

options.label: Fibres that tire quickly are simply older than the ones that last
options.feedback: The difference between fatigue-resistant and quickly-tiring fibres isn't a matter of age; it's a matter of how each type is built to work.

options.label: Only the length of a fibre determines how quickly it tires
options.feedback: Length isn't the property that decides this; it's the internal make-up of the fibre, suited either to sustained gentle work or brief powerful bursts.

items.ok_line: Different fibre types are built for different jobs.
items.ko_title: Not blood flow, age, or length
items.ko_line: The difference lies in how the fibre itself is built, not in these.
items.exp_title: Two different kinds of fibre in the same muscle
items.exp_text: A single muscle is not made of one uniform kind of fibre; it is a mix of different types, each built for a different job. Some fibres are built to contract with modest force but keep going for a long stretch without tiring, well suited to steady effort held over time. Others are built to contract with far more force and speed but exhaust their local resources quickly, well suited to a short, powerful burst rather than a long, steady effort.

items.prompt: Why does the body of someone who repeatedly performs long, hard physical effort gradually become better able to sustain it?

options.label: The muscle fibres themselves change from the fast, powerful type into the slow, enduring type
options.feedback: Fibres do not switch wholesale from one type to the other this way; what changes is how well-supplied and efficient the existing fibres become.

options.label: The lungs permanently grow larger to hold more air
options.feedback: The volume of the lungs themselves does not keep increasing with repeated effort; the improvements that matter happen mostly at the level of the muscle being supplied.

options.label: The muscles grow more small blood vessels and more of the internal structures that use oxygen to release energy, improving how efficiently they're supplied
options.feedback: That denser network of small blood vessels and internal structures is exactly what improves the muscle's supply and efficiency.

options.label: The heart simply beats faster all the time, even at rest
options.feedback: A heart that adapts to repeated hard effort typically settles into a steadier, unhurried rhythm at rest, not a permanently faster one.

items.ok_line: More small vessels and more of those internal structures improve the supply.
items.ko_title: Not bigger lungs or a faster resting heart
items.ko_line: The lasting change happens at the level of the muscle's own supply, not the lungs or a racing resting heart.
items.exp_text: Repeated demanding effort is a signal to the body that its current supply lines to the working muscles aren't quite generous enough for what's being asked of them. In response, the muscle tissue grows a denser network of small blood vessels threading through it, bringing fuel and oxygen closer to more fibres at once, along with more of the tiny internal structures that use that oxygen to release usable energy. None of the fibres change what they fundamentally are; they simply become better supplied and more efficient at the job they already do.

items.prompt: Why can a long, sustained physical effort suddenly feel dramatically harder partway through, even without slowing down beforehand?

options.label: The nerves controlling the muscle suddenly go numb
options.feedback: Nerves keep functioning normally through this shift; what has changed is the fuel available to the muscle, not the nerve signals reaching it.

options.label: The muscle has simply reached its maximum possible size
options.feedback: Muscle size doesn't change over the course of one sustained effort; the sudden difficulty is about a fuel supply running low, not about the muscle's physical size.

options.label: The joints involved abruptly stiffen from lack of movement
options.feedback: This happens during continuous movement, not stillness, so stiff joints from inactivity aren't the explanation.

options.label: A store of readily available fuel inside the muscle runs low, and once it does, the muscle has to switch to less accessible sources
options.feedback: That switch to a slower, less convenient fuel source is exactly why the effort suddenly feels so much harder.

items.ok_title: Running out of the near fuel
items.ok_line: Switching to a slower fuel source is what makes it feel so much harder.
items.ko_title: Not the nerves, size, or joints
items.ko_line: The sudden difficulty traces back to fuel, not to nerves, muscle size, or the joints.
items.exp_title: Running out of the fuel closest at hand
items.exp_text: A working muscle keeps a store of fuel close by that it can draw on quickly, and for a long stretch of steady effort that store is what carries most of the load. Once that nearby store runs low, the muscle has to lean more heavily on fuel that takes longer to access and convert, and the effort that felt manageable a moment earlier can suddenly feel far heavier. The muscle hasn't failed; it has simply switched to a slower, less convenient way of getting the energy it still needs.

items.prompt: Why does the body rely more on fat as fuel during a long, gentle effort, but lean on quickly available fuel during a short, intense one?

options.label: Fat is only used once the muscles are completely exhausted
options.feedback: Fat is drawn on throughout gentle sustained effort from fairly early on, not only as some kind of last resort after exhaustion.

options.label: Carbohydrate stores are used only during sleep, never during exercise
options.feedback: Stored carbohydrate is exactly what gets drawn on heavily during intense exercise; it isn't reserved for sleep.

options.label: The choice between the two depends only on how warm the muscle is
options.feedback: Muscle temperature isn't what decides which fuel is favoured; it's the intensity and pace of the effort being demanded that decides it.

options.label: Fat releases energy slowly but in great supply, suiting gentle sustained effort, while stored carbohydrate can be broken down much faster to match a high-intensity demand
options.feedback: That difference in release speed, slow but plentiful against fast but limited, is exactly why each fuel suits a different kind of effort.

items.ok_title: A slow fuel and a fast one
items.ok_line: Release speed, not temperature, decides which fuel gets used.
items.ko_line: Which fuel is favoured depends on the pace of the effort, not on these.
items.exp_title: A slow-burning fuel and a fast-burning one
items.exp_text: Fat can be broken down into usable energy only at a fairly gentle pace, but the body's fat stores are large, which makes it well suited to fuelling a long, steady effort without running low. Stored carbohydrate can be broken down far faster, releasing energy quickly enough to match the sudden high demand of an intense burst of effort, but the supply kept ready this way is comparatively small. Effort that is gentle and long draws mostly on the slow, plentiful fuel, while effort that is short and intense draws mostly on the fast, limited one.

items.prompt: Why do your movements get noticeably clumsier and less precise when a muscle is very tired?

options.label: Tired muscles simply stop responding to nerve signals altogether
options.feedback: A tired muscle still responds to signals; the response has become less precise, not absent.

options.label: A tired muscle responds to nerve signals less precisely, turning what should be smooth, graded contraction into something more erratic
options.feedback: That loss of precise, graded response is exactly what makes a tired movement feel clumsy.

options.label: Clumsiness at that point comes from the joints swelling up
options.feedback: Joints don't swell up from ordinary fatigue like this; the loss of coordination traces back to how the muscle is responding to signals, not to any swelling.

options.label: The eyes simply stop tracking movement accurately when tired
options.feedback: The clumsiness shows up even with the eyes closed, in movements guided without watching them at all, which points to the muscle's own response rather than to vision.

items.ok_line: The same signal now produces a less exact response.
items.ko_title: Not silence, swelling, or the eyes
items.ko_line: The muscle keeps responding, just less precisely; joints and eyes aren't the cause.
items.exp_title: A blunter response to the same signal
items.exp_text: A fresh muscle can turn a nerve signal into a finely graded contraction, producing exactly the amount of force and timing a smooth, controlled movement calls for. As fatigue sets in, that fine control breaks down: the same signal produces a response that is less exact, sometimes weaker than intended and sometimes stronger, arriving slightly out of step with what was meant. The instructions sent to the muscle haven't changed at all; what has changed is how faithfully the tired muscle can carry them out.

items.prompt: Why does a short pause during hard, repeated physical effort let you push through several more bursts than you could without any break at all?

options.label: A short pause resets the muscle completely back to a fresh state
options.feedback: A brief pause is nowhere close to a full reset; the muscle is still noticeably fatigued when the next burst begins, just somewhat less so than without any pause at all.

options.label: The pause lets a completely different set of muscle fibres take over the work
options.feedback: Largely the same fibres are called back into action after a short pause; what has changed for them is their state, not their identity.

options.label: A short pause allows some local fuel to be partly restored and some built-up byproducts to be partly cleared before the next burst begins
options.feedback: That partial restocking and partial clearing is exactly what gives the muscle a better starting point for the next burst.

options.label: Pausing works by cooling the muscle down to a lower temperature
options.feedback: A short pause is far too brief to meaningfully cool a working muscle; what it does in that time is chemical, not thermal.

items.ok_line: Partly restoring fuel and clearing byproducts is enough to help.
items.ko_title: Not a full reset, new fibres, or cooling
items.ko_line: The pause is too brief for any of those; what it buys is a partial chemical recovery.
items.exp_title: A partial reset, not a full one
items.exp_text: During a hard, repeated burst of effort, a muscle's local fuel gets used up and byproducts of that effort build up inside it, both of which make each successive burst harder than the last. Even a short pause gives the muscle a window to partly restock that local fuel and clear away some of the accumulated byproducts, without needing anywhere near full recovery to make a difference. That partial head start is enough to noticeably extend how many more bursts of hard effort the muscle can still deliver.
